model_selection_decision_evidence.rationale: The graph-retrieved candidates for object detection under a CPU-only, mid latency budget (<= 500 ms per image) and a target mAP@0.5:0.95 around 0.3 plus indoor furniture data point to YOLOv10 family as a balanced choice. The deterministic recommendation selects yolov10s as the architecture with a policy of balanced capacity and resource headroom, meaning it fits the hardware constraints (8 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM) and provides a practical margin for latency without overfitting to a small model. The memory footprint is modest: FP16 weights ~7.2M parameters for yolov10s with total VRAM need around 0.266 GB, plus activation workspace ~0.25 GB, totaling well within the available RAM for a typical CPU inference pipeline. Benchmark evidence shows COCO mAP50-95 around 46.8 with a 640 px input, which comfortably surpasses the target 0.3 threshold. CPU latency benchmarks for yolov10s on CPU are unverified in the graph, hence the unverified status for the max_cpu_latency_ms constraint. As a safety net, yolov10n (nano variant) is available as a lower compute fallback if the CPU latency validation on your hardware reveals tighter constraints than expected. The other YOLO and RT-DETR candidates either show higher CPU latency, larger memory footprints, or lack CPU latency verification within the 500 ms target window for a similar accuracy, making yolov10s the most practical single architecture under the stated constraints. In indoor furniture detection, you may later fine-tune on the openimages furniture subset or similar indoor datasets to further align with your domain. Local constraint validation replaced the agent choice 'yolov10' with 'yolov10s'.

Model Selection Rationale: The graph-retrieved candidates for object detection under a CPU-only, mid latency budget (<= 500 ms per image) and a target mAP@0.5:0.95 around 0.3 plus indoor furniture data point to YOLOv10 family as a balanced choice. The deterministic recommendation selects yolov10s as the architecture with a policy of balanced capacity and resource headroom, meaning it fits the hardware constraints (8 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM) and provides a practical margin for latency without overfitting to a small model. The memory footprint is modest: FP16 weights ~7.2M parameters for yolov10s with total VRAM need around 0.266 GB, plus activation workspace ~0.25 GB, totaling well within the available RAM for a typical CPU inference pipeline. Benchmark evidence shows COCO mAP50-95 around 46.8 with a 640 px input, which comfortably surpasses the target 0.3 threshold. CPU latency benchmarks for yolov10s on CPU are unverified in the graph, hence the unverified status for the max_cpu_latency_ms constraint. As a safety net, yolov10n (nano variant) is available as a lower compute fallback if the CPU latency validation on your hardware reveals tighter constraints than expected. The other YOLO and RT-DETR candidates either show higher CPU latency, larger memory footprints, or lack CPU latency verification within the 500 ms target window for a similar accuracy, making yolov10s the most practical single architecture under the stated constraints. In indoor furniture detection, you may later fine-tune on the openimages furniture subset or similar indoor datasets to further align with your domain. Local constraint validation replaced the agent choice 'yolov10' with 'yolov10s'.
